summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, and Court of Cassation interpretations from the 1970s had already removed any requirement of financial exchange, so habitual or multiple partners alone suffices for conviction. Outright International's country overview (updated 12 March 2026) records that vague public-morality and debauchery provisions are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences.

Police run entrapment operations against visitors as well as residents. A BBC investigation documents officers using fake accounts on LGBTQ dating applications to identify, blackmail and arrest users, with victims describing detention after meetings arranged through those apps. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the same pattern, noting that entrapment targets transgender women in particular through fake profiles, and that violations continue inside police stations.

Arrest is frequently accompanied by coercive medical examination. Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing documents rising arrests of gay and trans people alongside forced anal examinations and authorities turning a blind eye to abuse in custody. Human Rights Watch, in "In a Time of Torture" (29 February 2004), documented arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings motivated by sexual orientation during the Queen Boat crackdown, with testimony from defendants. State officials and police are reported to harass, abuse and torture LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, producing unfair arrests and abuse in custody.

Legal gender recognition is being actively closed. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide in December 2024 removes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that had allowed transgender Egyptians to correct gender markers through governorate committees.

Expression and visibility carry their own exposure. The Supreme Media Regulatory Council ordered in 2017 that "the appearance of the homosexuals" and the promotion of their slogans be kept off air, and legislation introduced in August 2018 placed any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, television hosts incited violence against the community and one published personal information of flag-raisers; at least 84 people were arrested between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. Host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year in January 2019 for hosting a gay man on his programme.

There is no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. TIMEP's submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle (6 January 2025) records that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health, with barriers to equitable services persisting since the previous cycle and pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Personal and family law follows the religious law of the person's recognised religion, none of which recognises same-sex relationships, so Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. A public same-sex relationship can be entered as evidence in a criminal indictment under provisions against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality. Sentences reflect severity: in 2004 a seventeen-year-old student received 17 years' imprisonment, including two years' hard labour, for posting a profile on a gay dating site.
tangentialFactors:
Egypt's regime is unusual in that the criminal statutes do not name same-sex conduct, yet the practical outcome is explicit criminalisation: Economic Courts now read Penal Code provisions together with the Anti-Sex Work Law, and the Court of Cassation's 1970s interpretations had already removed the financial-exchange element. The gap between the letter of the law and enforcement is therefore narrower for a visitor than the absence of an express offence would suggest.

Social climate is hostile enough to shape enforcement. Polling cited in country coverage finds that 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and support for LGBTQ rights remains a minority position, which is why political parties and human rights organisations do not express public support. The derogatory term "khawalat", historically referring to male cross-dressing dancers, is applied to gay and gender-nonconforming men, and Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters almost exclusively through stereotyping and defamation.

The September 2017 rainbow flag incident produced a sustained period of arrests, media incitement and forced anal testing, and is described as causing trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ people, with multiple attempted suicides. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, was granted asylum in Canada and died by suicide in 2020. A December 2014 raid on a public bathhouse, organised with a television presenter, arrested around 26 men who were later acquitted; a newspaper was shut down and two reporters jailed in 2009 over a story about actors and homosexual prostitution; a comedian was charged in 2013 with propagating homosexuality and obscenity.

Earlier and later documentation points the same way. The 2004 Human Rights Watch report on the Queen Boat crackdown remains the reference account of torture and denial of justice in cases built on sexual orientation, and Outright International's 2026 overview finds the same vague morality provisions still in use.
localsOnly:
Transgender Egyptians lost the practical route to correcting gender markers on official documents in December 2024, when the Ministry of Interior issued a directive to civil-registry heads nationwide closing the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that had permitted corrections through governorate committees. Legal gender recognition is now being shut rather than expanded.

Residents face arrest under the debauchery and public-morality provisions rather than an express homosexuality offence, with Economic Courts convicting on the basis of habitual or multiple partners without any element of payment. Bedayaa documents rising arrests of gay and trans people, coerced anal examinations, and authorities turning a blind eye to abuse in custody; the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records entrapment through fake accounts on LGBTQ dating platforms, disproportionately targeting transgender women, and continuing violations inside police stations.

Personal and family status is governed by the religious law of the person's recognised religion, Islam or Coptic Orthodox Christianity, neither of which recognises same-sex relationships, so marriage is available only between a man and a woman. Where a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in an indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.

There is no anti-discrimination law or policy covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. In healthcare, transgender and intersex Egyptians encounter discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health, with barriers persisting across UPR cycles and discrimination in medical settings described as pervasive.

Media and online expression are constrained for residents: a 2017 regulatory order bars the appearance of homosexual people and the promotion of their slogans in media, and since August 2018 any social network user with more than 5,000 followers falls under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. Hosting a gay guest on television resulted in a one-year prison sentence in January 2019.
outOfScopeNotes:
The December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive closing the gender-marker correction route is sourced to a single Cairo 52 report; its current implementation status across governorates, and whether any committee route survives in practice, is unresolved in the available inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses how Egyptian border and consular officers treat a passport whose sex marker has been changed, or whether a mismatch between passport marker and presentation triggers additional screening at entry. That question is not sourced here.

The inventory does not establish whether the coercive anal examinations documented by Bedayaa and Human Rights Watch continue under a current standing instruction or occur case by case; the sources record their use in specific arrest waves without stating present policy.

TIMEP's January 2025 submission frames health-access barriers as persisting since the previous UPR cycle, but the inventory contains no record of what recommendations Egypt received or accepted in its fourth cycle, so the status of that review process is unresolved.

Whether the deportation practice documented by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and the Cairo 52 incident count has any published appeal or consular-notification mechanism is not stated in the sources.
